opus-5.5.text:
Well, it's a slightly awkward position for me, being one of the people who worked on the original Transformer paper and now going around saying we should probably move on from it. But I think that's exactly why I feel comfortable saying it.

What worries me is that the field has become very narrow. When the Transformer came out, there was a lot of exciting architectural exploration happening: people were trying all sorts of recurrent variants, memory-augmented networks, different kinds of attention. Then the Transformer worked so well, and scaled so well, that almost all of that energy collapsed into one direction. Now, if you're a researcher with a genuinely new architectural idea, you're competing against something that has had years of engineering, hardware co-design, and enormous compute poured into it. Even a fundamentally better idea might look worse at first, so it gets abandoned. We may be stuck in a local optimum, and the success of the current approach is part of what keeps us there.

There are also signs that something is missing. These models can be astonishingly capable and then fail in ways that feel very unhuman. They make strange, brittle mistakes. They don't really reason in a way that adapts its effort to the problem; the amount of computation per token is basically fixed by the architecture. We've added tricks on top, like chain-of-thought and longer inference, which help, but they feel like patches rather than something built into how the model thinks.

So I'm interested in ideas that take more inspiration from biology, like the timing and synchronization of neurons, or models that can think for a variable amount of time internally before answering. I'm not claiming any one of those is the answer. My point is that we should be exploring much more broadly, because I'd be surprised if the architecture we happened to land on in 2017 is the final one.

r001.rationale: It says these models do not adapt their computational effort to the problem and points to variable internal thinking time, clearly conveying that reasoning needs adaptive computation.

r002.rationale: It calls chain-of-thought and longer inference “patches” added on top, contrasting them with capabilities built into how the model thinks.

fable-5.1.text:
I think the honest answer is that we got lucky with the transformer, and then the field got a bit stuck on it. When we wrote the attention paper, nobody thought this was the final architecture. It was a good engineering solution to a specific problem, which was that recurrent models were slow to train because you couldn't parallelize across the sequence. Attention solved that. It let us throw enormous amounts of compute at the problem, and scaling did the rest.

But that's the thing, scaling did the rest. Most of the progress since then has come from making the same basic machine bigger and feeding it more data, not from the architecture itself getting smarter. And when you look at what the model actually does at inference time, it's a fixed amount of computation per token regardless of how hard the question is. If I ask it what two plus two is or ask it to prove a theorem, it spends roughly the same effort on the next token. That feels wrong. Biological systems don't work that way, and I don't think a system that genuinely reasons should work that way either. Chain of thought and all the test-time compute tricks are, in a sense, patches on top of this. They're the model externalizing a loop that arguably should be internal.

The other thing that bothers me is that these models don't learn once they're deployed. Training and inference are completely separate phases. You compress the world into the weights, you freeze them, and then the model has to make do with whatever fits in the context window. There's no mechanism for it to adapt, to consolidate experience, to change the way it's thinking based on what it just encountered. The context window is a bit of a crutch there too, because attention over a long context is expensive and, frankly, a brute force way to handle memory.

So when I say fundamental changes, I mean things like adaptive computation, where the model decides how long to think. Some form of continual learning so the system is actually evolving rather than being frozen. And honestly, I'd like to see more of the field explore things that aren't trained purely by gradient descent on a giant static dataset, because I suspect the training procedure matters as much as the architecture. One of the reasons I left Google to start Sakana was exactly this, to have the freedom to look at nature-inspired approaches, evolutionary methods, collective intelligence, things that don't fit the current paradigm. Not because I'm sure they'll win, but because almost everyone else is making the same bet on the same architecture, and I think that's a risky place for a field to be.

r001.rationale: It argues that genuine reasoning should use variable effort and explicitly calls for adaptive computation, where the model decides how long to think.

r002.rationale: It calls chain-of-thought and test-time compute tricks patches on top of the architecture, and says the reasoning loop should be internal.

astra-6.text:
I think we’ve become very good at making one particular approach work, and that can make it harder to explore alternatives. Once you have an architecture that scales predictably, there’s a strong incentive to spend your resources scaling it rather than asking whether its basic assumptions are right.

With a language model, for example, we tend to tie the amount of computation to the number of tokens. But the difficulty of a problem doesn’t necessarily have much to do with how long the question is. You might have a very short question that requires a tremendous amount of thought. Generating intermediate steps helps, but I think there’s still a more fundamental question about how a model should decide what computation to do and when to stop.

That doesn’t mean the Transformer has hit a wall. I wouldn’t claim that. It means that improving the current recipe and discovering a better recipe are different research activities, and we need room for both. A new idea will probably look worse initially, because it hasn’t had years of engineering and tuning behind it. If we insist that every experiment immediately beats the best existing system, we’ll filter out a lot of potentially interesting directions.

r001.rationale: It says a model should decide what computation to do and when to stop, and contrasts that with computation tied to token count.

r002.rationale: It questions current architectural assumptions and says intermediate steps help, but does not criticize adding capabilities onto language-model architectures instead of building them in intrinsically.

sol-6.1.text:
I think we’ve got very good at making the same basic architecture bigger, but that doesn’t necessarily mean we’ve found the right architecture. Scaling gives you a very reliable way to improve things, which makes it harder to justify trying something fundamentally different. If your new idea doesn’t work immediately, you can always go back to the transformer and spend more compute.

What interests me is whether we’re missing mechanisms that would let these systems learn and use information more efficiently. There’s a difference between getting better because you’ve absorbed more examples and getting better because you have a better way of solving the problem. Those aren’t mutually exclusive, but I don’t think we should assume that scaling the current approach will give us every capability we want.

That doesn’t mean throwing the transformer away. It means leaving room for experiments where the payoff is uncertain, because a genuinely different approach probably won’t look competitive on day one.

r001.rationale: The response discusses learning and using information efficiently, but does not state that reasoning requires adaptive computation.

r002.rationale: The response questions reliance on scaling and calls for exploring different architectures, but does not criticize adding capabilities onto existing architectures or say they should be provided intrinsically.
